results.content:
Title: Curated AWS SSM Scripts
We’ve written in a previous article about Rewind’s use of AWS SSM Session Manager and associated IAM policies to allow shell and SSH tunnel access to AWS resources. AWS Systems manager has a feature called Run Commands which allow you to run scripts or commands on EC2 instances that have the SSM agent installed. SSM documents can be invoked via the AWS console by selecting the document and choosing **run command** or it can be invoked using the CLI or API. While the above sample document shows a script embedded in an SSM document, it is possible to have an SSM document reference code in Github directly (either public or private repos). How does an SSM document look when it’s pulling code from Github? "Resource": "arn:aws:ssm:*:*:document/scripts-read-only-*",. The first block allows access to SSM documents beginning with the prefix _scripts-read-only-._ Users (or roles) with this policy block will only be able to run documents that are named beginning with _scripts-read-only-_. Using combinations of these blocks assigned to different IAM users/groups/roles, you can restrict access to specific SSM documents and EC2 instances. But how can we automatically translate code in a private Github repo to SSM documents automatically? We’ve created a publicly available Github action which automatically creates SSM documents for code added to a Github repo. This action will generate the correct YAML for the SSM document and fill in the correct script name to execute. uses: rewindio/github-action-generate-ssm-documents@main. In this example, SSM documents will be created for any files checked into the repo and pushed to the us-east-1 and eu-west-1 regions. We want to generate SSM documents for each file changed. uses: rewindio/github-action-generate-ssm-documents@main. This is our Github action that generates the SSM document(s) for each changed file. The AWS keys referenced must be stored as Github encrypted secrets for the repo and the corresponding AWS IAM user must have enough permissions to be able to upload SSM documents (ideally no more than this). _Whenever files are added to this github repo under the scripts folder, a corresponding SSM document will be created in the us-east-1 and eu-west-1 regions._. Here’s a sample IAM policy that we’ll step through: The first block allows access to SSM documents beginning with the prefix *scripts-read-only-.*  Users (or roles) with this policy block will only be able to run documents that are named beginning with *scripts-read-only-*. This is controlled at the IAM Group level and the appropriate IAM policy assigned for the subset of curated scripts we want to allow access to ## Auto-Generating and Publishing SSM Documents We have most of the pieces of this solution in place now. We’ve created a publicly available Github action which automatically creates SSM documents for code added to a Github repo. Here’s a sample workflow (this goes in your .github/workflows folder in the Github repo containing your scripts) In this example, SSM documents will be created for any files checked into the repo and pushed to the us-east-1 and eu-west-1 regions. This is our Github action that generates the SSM document(s) for each changed file. The AWS keys referenced must be stored as Github encrypted secrets for the repo and the corresponding AWS IAM user must have enough permissions to be able to upload SSM documents (ideally no more than this) So putting this all together in a simple “what does this do” statement: *Whenever files are added to this github repo under the scripts folder, a corresponding SSM document will be created in the us-east-1 and eu-west-1 regions.* ## Invoking Documents using aws-connect The final piece of our solution is an easy way to execute these scripts.

# Unit Testing Your Vector Config Files. Treating your Vector configuration files as code. Today we’re excited to announce beta support for unit testing Vector. configurations, allowing you to define tests directly within your Vector. These tests are used to assert the output from topologies of. transform components given certain input events, ensuring. that your configuration behavior does not regress; a very powerful feature for. mission-critical production pipelines that are collaborated on. ## Example. Let’s look at a basic example that uses the `regex_parser`. transform to parse log lines:. include = ["/var/log/my-app.log"]. value = "2019-11-28T12:00:00+00:00 info Hello world". "timestamp.equals" = "2019-11-28T12:00:00+00:00". And you can run the tests via the new `test` subcommand:. Many Vector configurations will be simple transformations across straight. forward pipelines (such as tailing a file and piping the. data to AWS CloudWatch Logs) and don’t really. However, Vector configs are capable of. expanding indefinitely with transforms in order to solve as. much of your processing needs as possible. As a configuration grows, and as the number of owners of a configuration grow, the potential. for regressions also grows just like a regular code base. capabilities of configuration driven services is therefore a common pain for. We hope that natively supporting unit tests in Vector. configs will preemptively solve this problem. ## Getting Started. To help you get started we put together two documentation pages:.
